newsitem.title: USA: Strange vendetta fuels Alaska Senate challenge.
newsitem.headline: Strange vendetta fuels Alaska Senate challenge.

text.p: Tom Obermeyer failed the Alaska bar exam for the 22nd time this year -- the result, his wife insists, of a conspiracy involving Sen. Ted Stevens, judges, Alaska's Jewish lawyers and the news media.
So Theresa Obermeyer is seeking to win revenge through the ballot box, running as the Democratic candidate against longtime Republican incumbent Stevens.

Her beliefs about a persecution plot dominated her stormy tenure on the Anchorage School Board, fuelling her frequent outbursts at public events and repeated arrests for disorderly conduct that resulted in a month-long jail term this year.

But thanks to a dearth of mainstream contenders willing to take on the powerful Stevens, Obermeyer emerged from a field of seven candidates to win the Democratic primary. She is expected to finish third in Tuesday's general election behind Stevens and Green Party candidate Jed Whittaker.
In a televised debate this week, the raspy-voiced Obermeyer repeated her accusations to Stevens. "I have been attacked mercilessly by you and your henchmen," she said.
Stevens, saying he is mystified at the charges, suggested Obermeyer may be mentally unstable. "I wish you'd go find some help. I think you need help, Mrs. Obermeyer," he said.

Stevens ranks second in seniority among Senate Republicans and is in line to chair the powerful Appropriations Committee if his party retains control of the body. His 28-year tenure includes much success in securing generous federal funding for Alaska projects. That has inspired criticism from budget hawks, but Stevens defends the federal spending for Alaska.
"One man's pork is another man's beef," he has said.

One of the most popular politicians in state history, Stevens is expected to coast to an overwhelming victory. Establishment Democrats such as Gov. Tony Knowles and Fairbanks Mayor Jim Hayes have endorsed him and have worked hard to distance themselves from Obermeyer.

Whittaker, of the Green Party, opposes oil development in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, unlike most politicians in this petrodollar-dependent state. Instead he advocates development of natural-gas-fuelled vehicles to spur sales of natural gas from Alaska's North Slope.
He also endorses sovereignty for Alaska Natives, an end to clear-cutting in state forests and a $9-an-hour minimum wage.

Whittaker, a longshoreman, said he knows he has no chance of winning but hopes to spur discussion with his candidacy. "I am just a humble gardener. I plant seeds. I am here to try and protect the earth," he said in the debate.
Obermeyer, who refers to herself as a former political prisoner and who sometimes dons a striped jailbird costume for her public appearances, does enjoy wide name recognition.

"My style is not all confrontational. It is direct," she said, blaming her poor reputation on the state's news media. "That has all been very planned to make me look like I am not being intellectual, not professional," she said.
